name: Krambambula
description: Vodka and honey mulled with cinnamon, clove and nutmeg — a Belarusian recipe rescued from the eighteenth century and now a national symbol.
funFact: Krambambula was originally a Danzig cherry liqueur, but the Belarusian version — honey, spice and spirit, served hot — became a marker of national identity during the cultural revivals of the 1990s.

steps: Simmer the water, honey and all the spices together for 10 minutes.
Take the pan off the heat and let it cool for a few minutes.
Stir in the vodka off the heat.
Strain and serve hot in small mugs, or bottle it and reheat as needed.

name: Bevanda
description: Red wine cut with still water — the Dalmatian working drink, and a habit inherited more or less directly from the Romans.
funFact: Diluting wine with water was standard practice in the classical Mediterranean, where drinking it neat was considered barbaric; the Dalmatian coast simply never stopped.

steps: Pour the red wine into a plain tumbler.
Add still water to taste — roughly half and half for a working bevanda.
Stir once.
Serve at cellar temperature, with food.

name: Gemišt
description: White wine and sparkling mineral water. Croatia's default afternoon drink, and the reason Croatian mineral water brands are household names.
funFact: The ratio is regional and argued about — inland Croatia leans to half and half, while the coast pours a heavier wine measure and calls the weaker version an insult.

steps: Chill the wine and the mineral water.
Pour the wine into a tumbler.
Top with the sparkling mineral water.
Serve immediately; ice is a coastal habit and inland Croatia disapproves.

name: Beton
description: Becherovka and tonic — the Czech Republic's national mixed drink, named by acronym and tasting of cinnamon and gentian.
funFact: The name is an acronym of BEcherovka and TONic, and also happens to be the Czech word for concrete — a coincidence the marketing has always enjoyed.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Pour in the Becherovka and the lemon juice.
Top with cold tonic water.
Stir once and garnish with a lemon wedge.

name: Rakomelo
description: Cretan raki warmed with honey, cinnamon and clove. Served in winter, and pressed on you whether or not you asked.
funFact: In Crete, raki arrives free at the end of a meal whether you ordered it or not; rakomelo is the winter version, and refusing it is harder than it sounds.

steps: Warm the raki gently in a small pan with the cinnamon and cloves.
Stir in the honey until it fully dissolves.
Do not let it boil — you want it hot, not evaporating.
Strain into small heatproof glasses and serve at once.

name: Fröccs
description: Wine and soda, with an entire naming system attached: the ratio decides what you call it, and Hungarians know every name.
funFact: The vocabulary is exact: kisfröccs is 1 wine to 1 soda, nagyfröccs 2 to 1, hosszúlépés 1 to 2, and a házmester is 3 wine to 2 soda. There are at least a dozen more.

steps: Chill both the wine and the soda water thoroughly.
Pour the wine into a tumbler.
Add the soda water, adjusting the ratio to the fröccs you want.
Serve immediately, traditionally without ice.

name: Puszta Cocktail
description: Apricot brandy, Unicum and dry vermouth — bitter, stone-fruit and herbal, named for the Hungarian plain.
funFact: Unicum has been made by the Zwack family since 1790 from over forty herbs, and the family smuggled the recipe out of Hungary during the communist period, brewing a placebo version at home in the meantime.

steps: Combine all three in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 25 seconds until well chilled.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface.

name: Mad Dog
description: Vodka, raspberry syrup and Tabasco layered into one shot. Sweet, then red, then suddenly very hot. Polish student legend.
funFact: 'Wściekły pies' is a staple of Polish student bars, where the layering matters: the syrup sinks, the Tabasco floats, and the burn arrives a beat after the sweetness.

steps: Pour the raspberry syrup into the bottom of a shot glass.
Layer the vodka carefully over it with a barspoon.
Dash the Tabasco on top so it sits on the surface.
Drink in one — sipping it is a mistake people only make once.

name: Tatanka
description: Bison grass vodka and cloudy apple juice. Tastes like apple pie and freshly cut hay, which is a stranger compliment than it sounds.
funFact: Also called a Szarlotka, after the Polish apple cake. Żubrówka is flavoured with a blade of bison grass from the Białowieża Forest, and each bottle traditionally contains one.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Pour in the Żubrówka.
Top with cold cloudy apple juice.
Stir once and garnish with an apple slice and a light dusting of cinnamon.

name: Țuică Fiartă
description: Plum brandy heated with sugar and peppercorns until it steams. Romanian winter, taken standing outside in it.
funFact: The sugar is caramelised in the pan before the țuică goes in, which is what gives it the amber colour; the peppercorns are traditional and genuinely change the finish.

steps: Melt the sugar in a small pan over low heat until it just caramelises.
Add the peppercorns and cinnamon and stir for a few seconds.
Pour in the țuică carefully — it will spit — and warm it through without boiling.
Serve hot in small heatproof glasses.

name: Sbiten
description: Honey, spices and herbs simmered together and spiked — Russia's hot drink of choice for four centuries before tea arrived and took over.
funFact: Sbiten was street food in imperial Russia, sold from insulated copper samovar-like urns carried on the back; it was displaced almost entirely by tea in the nineteenth century.

steps: Bring the water and honey to a simmer, skimming any foam that rises.
Add the ginger, cinnamon, cloves and mint and simmer for 15 minutes.
Strain out the solids.
Stir in the wine or vodka off the heat if you want it alcoholic.
Serve very hot in mugs.

name: Yorsh
description: Vodka poured into beer. Named after a spiny river fish, and about as gentle as one.
funFact: The name comes from the ruffe, a small bristly fish — Russian drinkers use it as a warning label, since the mix is notorious for arriving all at once.

steps: Pour the beer into a mug, leaving room at the top.
Add the vodka directly to the beer.
Stir once, or drop the shot glass in whole for the theatrical version.
Drink promptly.

name: Bambus
description: Red wine and cola, half and half, over ice. Beloved across the Balkans and defended fiercely by everyone who drinks it.
funFact: The Balkan bambus predates Spain's kalimotxo in local memory by decades, and the two regions have never agreed on who got there first.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Pour in the red wine.
Top with cold cola.
Stir once and add a lemon slice if you want it sharper.

name: Tatratea Hot
description: Slovakia's herbal tea liqueur, served hot with honey and lemon. Comes in strengths from 22% to 72%, colour-coded by how serious you are.
funFact: The bottles are numbered by ABV — 32, 42, 52, 62, 72 — and the 72% 'Outlaw' edition exists mostly so that people can say they have had it.

steps: Put the honey and lemon slice in a warmed glass mug.
Add the hot water and stir until the honey dissolves.
Pour in the Tatratea and stir once.
Serve hot, with the lemon left in.

name: Horilka z Pertsem
description: Ukrainian vodka steeped with chilli and honey. Sweet at the front, hot at the back, drunk cold with something salted.
funFact: It is traditionally taken with salo — cured pork fat — on dark bread, a pairing that sounds unlikely and works because the fat blunts the burn.

steps: Put the chillies and peppercorns into a bottle of horilka.
Add the honey and shake until it dissolves.
Leave to infuse for three to seven days, tasting as you go — chillies work fast.
Strain out the solids once it is hot enough for you.
Serve ice cold in shot glasses.
